brief_text:
Armed Conflict & Security
• Shots were fired outside the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in Washington; President Trump and Vice President JD Vance were evacuated, a suspect was detained and no fatalities were reported, with one officer reportedly shot; video shows the suspect charging a security checkpoint as journalists described a chaotic scene.
• Trump later briefed reporters, sharing the suspect’s identity and video of the incident, and praised the rapid response of Secret Service agents.
• In Lebanon, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the IDF to “vigorously attack” Hezbollah despite a recently extended ceasefire, as strikes killed six people.
• Mali was rocked by one of its largest coordinated attacks in years, with gunfire and explosions across Bamako and other cities attributed to jihadist and separatist groups.
• A bomb-laden bus exploded on Colombia’s Pan-American Highway, killing at least 14, with authorities blaming a dissident FARC faction.
Why it matters: A string of violent incidents—from a high-profile U.S. security scare to intensified Middle East tensions and Sahel insurgent operations—highlights the fragility of security environments and risks of broader escalation.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Trump canceled a planned trip to Pakistan by his envoys for Iran ceasefire talks, stalling efforts to consolidate a truce and signaling diplomatic friction.
• Hundreds protested in Tel Aviv as US-Iran talks faltered, reflecting fears that hostilities could resume.
• EU leaders convened in Cyprus to coordinate Middle East strategy and push for an end to the Iran war.
• In Hungary, Viktor Orbán declined to take his parliamentary seat after a landslide defeat; incoming premier Peter Magyar warned investors to avoid Orban-linked assets amid claims of capital flight.
• Mexico said two Americans reportedly working for the CIA who died after a drug-lab raid were not authorized to operate in the country.
Why it matters: Diplomatic setbacks over Iran and political transitions in Europe could reshape regional security dynamics and investment risks.

Climate & Environment
• Venice is subsiding as seas rise; a review of proposed fixes finds no plan would preserve the city in its current form.
• ICE plans a family detention facility on a highly PFAS-contaminated Louisiana site, raising public health concerns.
• Research suggests criminalizing UK climate protesters is counterproductive, increasing activists’ determination to take direct action.
• California’s $114m wildlife crossing nears completion, touted as a model for reconnecting habitats amid controversy.
• Short-tailed shearwaters are washing up dead on Australian beaches in numbers tied to non-natural causes, underscoring marine ecosystem stress.
Why it matters: Environmental decisions—from infrastructure to policing protests—carry immediate health, legal and biodiversity consequences as climate pressures mount.

Society & Human Rights
• Rights groups say Venezuela’s amnesty has slowed, leaving more than 500 political prisoners still behind bars.
• Suicide-related callouts to fire services in England tripled over a decade, prompting calls for mandatory mental health training for first responders.
• In a rare interview, the RSS’s second-in-command defended the Indian group’s ideology amid scrutiny of Hindu nationalism.
• OpenAI’s CEO apologized to a Canadian community for not alerting authorities about a mass shooting suspect tied to its platform.
• The Kremlin is tightening control over book publishing, targeting even loyal houses, the FT reports.
Why it matters: Human rights, public safety and corporate accountability remain in sharp focus as societies navigate polarization and state pressure.

• The London Marathon returns with global streaming options for U.S.-based viewers.
• Formula 1 will return to Istanbul Park in 2027 under a new five-year agreement.
• The Fitzpatrick brothers shot a record 57 to lead the Zurich Classic, while Nelly Korda takes a five-shot lead into the Chevron Championship’s final day.
Why it matters: High-profile injuries and schedule changes shape club and national outcomes, while marquee events and records sustain fan interest and sponsorships.

Economy & Markets
• UK government departments differ widely on AI datacentre energy forecasts, exposing gaps between net-zero planning and digital ambitions.
• The Hormuz disruption has deepened a historic shipping crisis; clearing mines could take weeks even with allied support.
• Pistachio prices are jumping as Iran’s export routes are squeezed, while demand from Dubai’s growing chocolate sector rises.
• A wave of used EVs coming off lease through 2027 could drive down prices; Xiaomi accelerates its premium EV push into Europe.
• The Fed and other G7 central banks are poised to hold rates as energy costs threaten inflation; Hong Kong tops global IPO proceeds with $17.9bn year-to-date.
Why it matters: Energy constraints, geopolitics and technology adoption are reshaping supply chains, consumer prices and capital markets.

Health & Pandemic
• Dozens of MPs oppose granting the UK health secretary power to override NICE on drug costs, amid questions about legality and benefits to big pharma.
• NHS leaders warn Gulf shipping disruptions are threatening supplies of petrochemicals critical to single-use medical items and pharmaceuticals.
• Expert commentary stresses that high LDL cholesterol remains a serious cardiovascular risk despite alternative theories.
Why it matters: Policy shifts and supply chain risks could affect treatment access and costs in already strained health systems.

Science & Technology
• The US and China are ramping up rival crewed lunar programs, with analysts warning Beijing could land first; meanwhile, Artemis II set a new distance record.
• Reports say the Trump administration dismissed the entire National Science Board, intensifying concerns over federal science governance and funding.
• Maine’s governor vetoed a statewide moratorium on new data centers, reflecting tensions over AI infrastructure, power use and local impacts.
• Apple under incoming CEO John Ternus signals a hardware-forward strategy amid intensifying device competition.
• A new Hubble Space Telescope image captured from orbit marked its 36th birthday, as astronomers published fresh insights into why starburst galaxies “switch off.”
Why it matters: Policy, infrastructure and corporate direction will shape the pace and priorities of innovation from labs to lunar bases.

Artificial Intelligence
• Anthropic tested an online marketplace where AI agents acted as buyers and sellers of real goods with real money, exploring autonomous commerce.
• Cohere is merging with Germany’s Aleph Alpha, backed by Schwarz Group, to build a European “sovereign” AI option for enterprises.
• Google Cloud is banking on in-house AI chips and models to narrow its gap with AWS and Microsoft as investors assess higher-risk “neoclouds.”
• The AI talent war intensifies as senior software executives jump to OpenAI; Tesla’s in-car Grok chatbot shows both promise and safety concerns.
• Legal and ethical debates deepen over whether opaque AI systems can meet anti-discrimination standards.
Why it matters: Strategic alliances, infrastructure bets and real-world deployments will determine competitive advantage and public trust in AI.

Entertainment
• High winds prompted a temporary evacuation at Stagecoach before the festival resumed with delays; some sets were canceled and others pushed back.
• Star Trek: Strange New Worlds set a July 23 Season 4 premiere and released a teaser; House of the Dragon teased a “more brutal” Season 3.
• Prime Video dropped the Spider-Noir trailer starring Nicolas Cage; Hazbin Hotel was renewed for a fifth and final season.
• The Michael Jackson biopic is tracking toward a record musical biopic opening even as legal and editorial changes fueled controversy.
• Helena Bonham Carter exited The White Lotus Season 4 days into filming; the role will be reworked and recast.
Why it matters: Weather risks, franchise momentum and production shake-ups influence release schedules, marketing investments and audience engagement.

• August Wilson’s “Joe Turner’s Come and Gone” returns to Broadway with Taraji P. Henson and Cedric the Entertainer leading a widely praised ensemble.
• Director Barry Levinson reflects on the enduring controversy surrounding 1996’s “Sleepers” three decades later.
• Bottega Veneta showcased Kwangho Lee’s “Lightful” installation at Milan Design Week, blending fashion and craft through woven forms.
Why it matters: Revivals and cross-disciplinary collaborations keep classic themes and new aesthetics in dialogue, sustaining cultural renewal.

Climate & Environment.text: Unhindered by critics who called the $114m project ‘a bridge to nowhere’, a gigantic throughway allowing animals to cross a busy freeway is close to completionAtop a gigantic wildlife bridge in California this week, butterflies filled the air. A red-tailed hawk sailed above as a slight breeze ruffled the 6,000 native plants, including poppies and purple sage. You’d never guess that below the quiet expanse of rocks and plants, a 10-lane freeway ferries 400,000 cars each day.When the project broke ground four years ago, enthusiasm was high. The wildlife crossing in northern Los Angeles county would be the largest of its kind in the world, providing safe passage for mountain lions, bobcats and lizards. Continue reading...

Sports.title: The Turkish Grand Prix Is Officially Returning Starting 2027
Sports.text: SummaryFormula 1 will return to Istanbul Park in 2027 following a new five-year agreement that secures the Turkish Grand Prix through the 2031 seasonThe circuit joins Portugal's Portimao as a returning venue, while the Dutch Grand Prix is set to leave the calendar and races in Spa and Barcelona move to a biannual rotationF1 leadership emphasized the strategic importance of the Turkish market and the technical challenge of the track, specifically its legendary multi-apex Turn 8Formula 1 is officially bringing the heat back to Istanbul Park. Starting in 2027, the Turkish Grand Prix will reclaim its spot on the motorsport calendar, backed by a fresh five-year agreement that locks the race down through the 2031 season. This massive move confirms a long-term commitment to a venue that previously stepped up as an absolute fan-favorite stopgap during the heavily disrupted 2020 and 2021 campaigns. Originally cementing its reputation between 2005 and 2011, the circuit is widely revered by the modern grid for its aggressive, tire-punishing layout. The agreement was formally stamped in Turkey, featuring direct participation from F1 President Stefano Domenicali and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.The circuit itself is not just another track; it represents one of the most demanding technical tests in the entire sport. Drivers consistently praise the sheer physicality of its high G-force corners. The undisputed crown jewel of the complex remains its legendary, multi-apex Turn 8—a relentless left-hander that pushes both human endurance and aerodynamic engineering to their absolute limits. By locking in the event for the foreseeable future, Formula 1 leadership is sending a clear message about the strategic importance of the Eurasian market while answering the persistent call from fans for authentic, driver-focused arenas.While the 2027 master schedule will maintain a strict 24-race limit, the addition of Turkey alongside Portugal’s Portimao forces major structural shifts to the traditional European tour. The Dutch Grand Prix is slated to exit the rotation entirely to make room for these returning heavyweights. Meanwhile, historic staple circuits like Belgium’s Spa-Francorchamps and Spain’s Barcelona will pivot to a biannual rotation format. This aggressive restructuring highlights a pivotal era for the championship as it balances legacy European roots with an ever-expanding global footprint.The evolution of the global tour refuses to stop with these latest announcements. Beyond the confirmed return of the Turkish Grand Prix, the sport's governing body continues to navigate preliminary discussions regarding potential future race events in both Thailand and Africa. Securing an African Grand Prix has been a particularly vocal, public priority for seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton. As the calendar becomes increasingly saturated and competitive, these deliberate venue changes underscore a fierce battle for a spot on the most exclusive motorsport schedule in the world.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: There’s a Snake in My Crocs: Disney x Pixar x Crocs Debut Structural ‘Toy Story 5’ Collab
Entertainment.text: Name: Disney x Crocs Jessie Boot, Disney x Crocs Classic Clog Toy Story AlienColorway: Multi, MultiSKU: 213009-90H, 213010-90HMSRP: $130 USD, $70 USDRelease Date: June 16Where to Buy: CrocsDisney and Pixar are teaming up with Crocs to celebrate the premiere of Toy Story 5. Executing a two-piece drop centered around the beloved franchise, this release bypasses standard colorway updates to focus on structural modifications, delivering character-specific molded elements directly onto the brand's foundational foam silhouettes.Taking a departure from the traditional slip-on design, the "Jessie Boot" utilizes a taller, structural shaft crafted from the brand's core water-resistant foam. The boot's physical architecture is visually anchored by a molded cow-print pattern on the lower half, contrasted against a bright red upper section that directly references the character's recognizable western wear. Functional pull tabs at the collar and a rugged tread pattern on the outsole complete the utilitarian construction, while dedicated ports across the vamp allow for the integration of accompanying thematic Jibbitz charms.The Classic Clog "Alien" returns to the core mechanics of the standard Crocs model but heavily augments the upper with distinct, character-driven modifications. A bright green foam base serves as the primary structural layer, paired with a specialized pivoting heel strap designed for secure, everyday wear. The standout technical feature lies in the custom Jibbitz charm integration, which includes molded eyes, planetary insignias, and Pizza Planet-themed accessories that interact directly with the shoe's ventilated forefoot ports to complete the extraterrestrial aesthetic.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Bottega Veneta And Kwangho Lee Are a Match Made in Heaven
Art & Culture.text: Categorisation doesn't really work for Kwangho Lee. His work, spanning sculpture, design and material experimentation, has never settled comfortably into a single discipline, so instead, he moves between them. Simple.  However, that doesn’t mean he lacks an aesthetic or red thread. Weaving, in particular, underpins much of what he does, and is the focus for his "Lightful", his latest installation for Bottega Veneta, presented during Milan Design Week.After studying Metal Art & Design at Hongik University, Lee’s projects went on to incorporate everything from industrial wire to organic fibres, often pushing familiar techniques into less predictable territory. Within Bottega Veneta, that experimental mindset is applied to leather, specifically through its signature Intrecciato.“I felt a strong desire to be more assertive,” he says. “I have always defined my artistic identity through the technique of weaving, it is the medium through which I communicate my thoughts and my very existence.”The installation consists of a series of suspended woven forms that vary in scale and density. Some appear loose and open, with strands extending outward; others are more compact, forming heavier, more structured volumes. Rather than presenting a single focal point, the work unfolds across the space.“For this collaboration, it wasn't simply a matter of transporting a finished piece into the venue,” Lee explains. “It required a profound understanding of both the collaboration and the physical space itself.”While the initial concept was developed in advance, the final composition took shape on site. Lee describes the process as one of “experimentation and dialogue,” responding to the architecture of the store and adjusting the work in real time, “the definitive completion of my work only truly happens on-site with people,” he adds.As for the installation’s title, it comes from the fact that light plays a central role in how it is  experienced. Shadows and highlights alter the apparent density and scale of each piece, with natural light changing how it appears throughout the day. Lightful continues the ongoing collaboration between Lee and Bottega Veneta. This is their third project together, following earlier work that included runway elements and participation in the Weaving the World exhibition in Seoul. In preparation, Lee visited the brand’s atelier in Montebello Vicentino, gaining a closer understanding of its production methods and craftsmanship.In a world saturated with forced collaboration, the fact that Lee has spent time with the brand is evident. Lightful is unmistakably Lee’s work, but it also totally remains grounded in the technical precision associated with the house. The result is a balance between experimentation and control, where traditional techniques are extended rather than replaced.He then invites the visitor to become the third collaborator: “rather than embedding ‘hidden details’ for people to solve,” Lee says, “I want my work to act as a catalyst. I want people to encounter these woven forms and feel something entirely their own.”Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
